opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underrated things that's happened in the last couple of years. When you give a model a really long context, say hundreds of thousands or millions of tokens, its ability to pick up a new task purely from what's in that window is remarkable. In some respects it's already superhuman.

The example that stuck with me is from the Gemini 1.5 work. They put an entire grammar book and dictionary for a very low-resource language, one with only a few hundred speakers and essentially nothing on the internet, into the context. The model could then translate into and out of that language at roughly the level of a human who'd spent months studying the same materials. A person would take weeks to absorb that book. The model does it in one forward pass. That's a huge gap in sample efficiency, at least on the ingestion side.

So I'd frame it this way. People often say these models are terrible learners because pre-training needs trillions of tokens while a kid needs far less. That's true of the gradient-descent part. But in-context learning is a different regime. Within the context window the model can be extraordinarily sample-efficient. It can hold far more information in active working memory than any human, cross-reference all of it at once, and draw on it immediately.

Where humans still clearly win is persistence and integration over time. If I spend six months at a new job, I gradually build a rich, compressed model of the codebase, the people, and the unwritten norms. That knowledge sticks, and it changes how I think about everything else. The model's in-context learning disappears when the context ends, and it's not obvious it's doing the deep restructuring a human does, as opposed to very good lookup and pattern-matching over what's in the window. There's also some degradation over really long contexts. The model can find a needle in a haystack, but reasoning coherently over all of it at once is harder.

Overall, I think long context is a big piece of the puzzle for making these systems useful as agents and coworkers. A lot of what feels like "the model isn't smart enough" is really "the model doesn't have the context a human employee would have." As context gets longer and models use it better, many of those gaps close without the underlying model needing to get much smarter. The remaining open question is how you get that learning to accumulate and persist, rather than resetting every time.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that long-context models are already surprisingly good at learning new tasks in context, in some narrow sense better than humans, and in other senses still clearly worse.

Where they're better: if you drop a million tokens of a codebase or a new language's grammar into the context, the model can pick up patterns and conventions almost instantly. The classic example people point to is Gemini learning Kalamang from a grammar book and a dictionary, a language with essentially no presence on the internet, and getting to a reasonable translation quality in a single forward pass. A human linguist given the same materials would take weeks. So the raw ability to absorb structure from a pile of text and start using it is really strong, and it scales well with context length.

Where they're worse: the learning is shallow in a particular way. In-context learning is more like very fast pattern matching than the kind of consolidation a human does. If you work with someone for a week on a new task, by the end they've built a compressed model of it. They know what matters and what doesn't, they've formed intuitions, they've changed. The model hasn't changed at all. Everything it "learned" lives in the activations and disappears when the context goes away. And within a long context, you also see the attention getting diluted, so the model's effective use of the information degrades somewhat as you pile more in. Needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks look saturated, but the harder tests, where you need to reason across many scattered pieces of the context, still show real gaps.

The other big difference is sample efficiency over time. Humans learn from very few examples but then keep improving with practice. Models learn fast from the context but plateau. They don't get better at the task the hundredth time you ask them than the tenth time, unless something about the prompt changes. Bridging that, whether through continual learning, memory systems, or just making in-context learning richer, is one of the things I think actually matters a lot for getting to agents that can do long-horizon work. Right now the model is a brilliant new hire on day one, every single day.

r003.rationale: The response does not conjecture that models could already learn Atari from action-labeled gameplay frames out of the box.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting distinction is between fitting a lot of information into context and actually learning from it. Those aren’t quite the same thing. A model can find a fact buried in a very long document, but that doesn’t establish that it can pick up a new skill from a sequence of experiences.

Humans are quite good at looking at a few examples, forming a hypothesis about what’s going on, and then asking a question that distinguishes between possible explanations. Models can do some of that, but they’re uneven. They might infer a complicated pattern immediately and then fail to incorporate a correction consistently.

So the test I’d want is: give a person and a model the same instructions for some unfamiliar task, let them try it, give them feedback, and see how their performance improves. Can they apply what they’ve learned to a case that looks different? Can they stop making the same mistake?

Long context gives you room to keep all those experiences around. The exciting question is whether the model can turn that history into progressively better behavior. I don’t think context length alone tells you the answer.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important distinction is between fitting a lot of information into the context and actually learning from it. If you give a model a million tokens of examples, can it infer the underlying task and then generalize to cases that look different? That’s a much stronger test than asking it to retrieve something from those tokens.

Humans are remarkably good at figuring out what matters from a few examples. But we also bring an enormous amount of prior experience, so it’s hard to make a fair comparison. Something that looks like learning a new task might mostly be recognizing a familiar structure.

What I’d want to see is a genuinely unfamiliar task, with examples and feedback, and then measure how performance improves as you give the model more experience. Does it correct a mistaken hypothesis? Can it use what it learned in a different setting? Long context makes that possible in principle, but the size of the context window alone doesn’t tell you how well the model learns.
